atoms.text: The notebook memory: a man with Alzheimer's stores directions in a notebook and trusts it as his own memory, so cognition is outsourced to an object.
The coupled system: mind, body, and environment function as one cognitive unit, so damaging the environment is brain damage.
The diary as identity: a person's sense of self depends on an external archive, so losing the archive is a kind of death.
The contested boundary: two people disagree over whether a tool is part of the mind or merely used by it, so personhood becomes a jurisdictional question.
The prosthetic cognition: a computer extends calculation beyond the skull, so intelligence is distributed and can be confiscated.
The shared memory: a group relies on a common external record, so forgetting becomes a collective failure rather than a private one.
The object that disagrees: an external memory returns information the person did not expect, so the extended mind can contradict its owner.
The search for the self in the environment: a person looks for who they are in their belongings, so identity is an archaeological dig.
The environment as accomplice: a room is arranged to make a decision inevitable, so architecture is a form of persuasion.
The lost phone: a person loses access to their calendar and becomes functionally amnesiac, so a device failure is a neurological event.
The two travelers: one remembers a route internally, the other reads it from a notebook, so the story asks whether the difference matters.
The externalized taboo: a culture stores its rules in objects and monuments, so morality is inherited as furniture.
The tool that edits back: an external memory is altered by someone else, so the person's past is revised without their knowledge.
The mind that spills: a person's thoughts leak into their environment and become readable, so privacy is a property of surfaces.
The archive that outlives: a notebook survives its owner and is read as a person, so the extended mind can persist after the brain stops.
The philosophical test: a thought experiment asks where the mind ends, so the story's conflict is a definition that cannot be settled by evidence.
